1 INTRODUCTION to ACCOUNTING

Terms you should know

Accounting equation — expresses the relationship between the amounts owned by the business and the
amounts owed by the business. Usually expressed as A = L + P or A =L + OE (owner's equity).

Assets — item of financial value owned or controlled by the business, it has future benefits for the business.
Entit; sumption — the affairs of the business and the affairs of the owner must be kept separate

Lial — amounts owed by a business

Owner's equity — the amount the business owes to the owner, and is equal to assets minus liabilities. Also
known as proprietorship or net worth.

Non current assets — items of value owned or controlled by the business that will be of benefit to the business

Non current liabilities — amounts owed by the business that will not need to be paid within the next 12 months

3 QUALITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS/PRINCIPLES

Terms you should know

QUALITATIVE CHARACTERISTICS

Comparability — ability to compare accounting information from one accounting period to another

Materiality — accounting information includes all information whose omission or misstatement would affect the
decisions of users

Relevance — inclusion of information that will influence the decisions of the users

Reliability ~ accounting information must represent the affairs of the business without bias or misstatement
Timeliness — reports must be prepared in sufficient time to form the basis of effective decisions
Understandability — the qualitative characteristic of reports that are easily understood by the users
PRINCIPLES

Accounting period (reporting period) — the period for which accounting reports are prepared, This cannot be
longer than 12 months.

Conservatism — income should not be included until earned but expenses should be included as soon as they
become liable. Profits should not be overstated.

Entity assumption — the affairs of the business and the affairs of the owner must be kept separate

Going concern — the business has a future life and will not cease in the foreseeable future

Historical cost — recording of assets at the price paid for them

Monetary - the principle of measuring all items in records and reports in a common monetary unit — eg Australian
dollars

Cash flow — cash coming into the business less the cash going out of the business

Debtors collections — the total of the amount collected (received) from debtors in the period

Creditors turnover — the length of time the business is taking to pay creditors. Measured by dividing the total

Debtors turnover — the length of time that the debtors are taking to pay. Measured by dividing total credit sales
by the average debtors

Quick asset ratio — measures the relationship between the quick assets (those than can be turned into cash
quickly) of a business and those current liabilities that must be paid in the very short term

‘Stock turnover — measures the length of time, on average, that the stock stays in the warehouse

Sufficient working capital ratio — the calculation of the working capital ratio taking into account the debtors,
creditors and stock turnovers

Working capital ratio — measures the relationship between the current assets and current liabilities of the
business

GLOSSARY

Accounting equation — expresses the relationship
between the amounts owned by the business and the
amounts owed by the business. Usually expressed as
A= L + OE (owner's equity) or A = L + P (proprietorship)

Accounting period — principle — the length of time for
which accounting reports are prepared. This cannot be

longer than one year.

Accrual accounting — an accounting method where
revenue is recorded and reported when earned (not
necessarily received) and expenses are recorded and
reported when incurred (not necessarily paid)

Accrued expenses — expenses that have been incurred
but are not yet paid. Classified as a current liability

Accrued revenue — revenues that have been earned, but
not yet received. Classified as a current asset.

Asset turnover — the relationship between the sales of
the business and the assets that were used while the
sales were made. Measures the sales per $ of assets
employed

Assets — items of financial value owned or controlled by
the business, which will assist it in earning revenue in the
future.

Bad debt — an amount that will not be received from a
credit customer.

Balance sheet — Statement of financial position — a
statement showing the assets, liabilities and owner's
equity of a business on a particular date.

Bank deposit form — document used to record deposits
at the bank

Bank overdraft — the withdrawals from the bank account
greater than the deposits into the account

Budgeting — planning. The preparation of forecast
statements for the business

Capital — the initial investment by the owner into the
business

Cash cycle — the time taken for cash outlaid by the
business to return as cash to the business

Cash flow — cash coming into the business less the cash
going out of the business

Cash register roll — the record of all cash received and
placed in the till

Cheque — an order from the owner of the account (the
payer) to the bank (drawer) to pay to the entity named
(the payee) the amount specified. Used to make most
cash payments for a business.

Comparability — qualitative characteristic — ability to
compare accounting information from one accounting
period to another

Concepts — see qualitative characteristics.

Conservatism — accounting principle — income should

© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92253 854 3

not be included until earned but expenses should be
included as soon as they become liable. Profits should
not be overstated.

Credit checks — checking of the financial viability of a
prospective customer before extending credit to them

Credit note — document used to record the return of
goods

Creditors turnover — the length of time the business is
taking to pay creditors, Measured by dividing the total
credit purchases by the average creditors.

Current assets — assets that are expected to be of
benefit to the business in the short term (less than
12 months)

Current liabilities — liabilities that must be paid within
12 months

Debt ratio — measures the relationship between the
assets of the business and the finance provided by
external parties.

Debtors collections — the total of the amount collected
(received) from debtors in the period.

Debtors turnover — the length of time that the debtors
are taking to pay. Measured by dividing total credit sales
by the average debtors.

Discount allowed/expense — an inducement to a debtor
to get them to pay their account quickly. It is a reduction
in the total owing.

Documents — evidence of transactions

Entity assumption — the affairs of the business and the
affairs of the owner must be kept separate

Equity ratio — measures the relationship between the
assets of the business and the amount contributed by the
owner.

Expense — cost incurred while earning revenue

Factoring — selling of debts (amounts owed by
customers) to a finance company to obtain cash from the
debts immediately

Gearing — the proportion of assets that have been
financed by external entities.

Going concern — accounting principle — the business
has a future life and will not cease in the foreseeable
future.

Gross profit ratio — the relationship between the sales
and the gross profit. Measure the amount of each $ of
sales that is retained as gross profit.

Historical cost — accounting principle — recording of
assets at the price paid for them

Income — revenue earned from the business activities of
the business

Interest cover — the number of times that the profit can
be divided by the interest expense.

>>P

Invoice — document used to record credit purchases or
sales.

Key performance indicators — KPIs — indicators used by
the management of the business to assess the success
of the trading operations. Non-ratio indicators.

Liabilities — amounts owed to an external entity

Liquidity — the ability of the business to pay its
short-term debts from its short-term resources

Loss — excess of expenses over revenues. Decreases
owner's equity.

Materiality — qualitative characteristic — accounting
information includes all information whose omission or
misstatement would affect the decisions of users.

Mortgage — a loan secured on property (usually having
been bought with the funds from the mortgage)

Net profit ratio — relationship between the sales and the
net profit. Measures the amount of each $ of sales that is
retained as net profit.

Net worth — assets minus liabilities

Non current assets — assets that will be of benefit to the
business in the long term

Non current liabilities — amounts that will have to be
paid in a period longer than 12 months

Opportunity cost — the cost of being involved in the
business opportunity. The benefit foregone by choosing a
particular alternative.

Owner's equity — the amount the business owes to the
‘owner, and is equal to assets minus liabilities. Also known
as Proprietorship or Net Worth.

Prepaid expenses — expenses that have been paid, but
not yet incurred. Classified as a current asset.

Prepaid revenue — revenue that has been received, but
not yet earned. Classified as a current liability.

Principles — guidelines, which assist in the accounting
system and reports to ensure that they are consistent
across time and consistent with other businesses.

Profit — excess of revenue over expenses.

Profit and loss statement — statement of financial
performance — a statement that lists all revenues and
expenses and shows the result of the trading activities of
a business for an accounting period. It is a summary
statement.

Profitability - measurement of the adequacy of the profit
received. It measures the effectiveness of the business in
using the resources available to it.

Proprietor — owner of the business

Proprietorship — Owner's equity, the amount that is
owed to the owner by the business. It is a residual of
assets minus liabilities.

Proprietary ratio — the relationship between the total

© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92253 854 3

Glossary (cont)

assets of the business and the amount contributed by the
owner.

Qualitative characteristics — guidelines for the
preparation of accounting records and reports so that
they represent the affairs of the business in a true and
fair manner.

Quick asset ratio — measures the relationship -between
the quick assets (those than can be turned into cash
quickly) of a business and those current liabilities that
must be paid in the very short term.

Receipt — document used to record the cash received
into a business.

Relevance — qualitative characteristic — inclusion of
information that will influence the decisions of the users.

Reliability — qualitative characteristic — accounting
information must represent the affairs of the business
without bias or misstatement.

Return on assets — measures the relationship between
net profit and the assets that were used to earn it.
Measures the amount of net profit per $ of assets
employed.

Return on owner's investment — measures the
relationship between the net profit and the amount of
owner's equity in the business.

Stability — the ability of the business to pay its debts in
the long term.

Statement of financial performance — profit and loss
statement ~ a statement that includes alll of the revenues
and expenses of the business in the accounting period
and is used to report on the profit or loss.

‘Statement of financial position — balance sheet — a
statement that includes all assets and liabilities of the
business and shows the owner's equity.

Stock loss — the stock in the warehouse is less than the
stock shown in the records.

Stock turnover — measures the length of time, on
average, that the stock stays in the warehouse.

Terms of trade — the terms on which the credit customer
has purchased the goods — for example, 2% discount if
paid in 10 days, net amount due in 30 days.

Timeliness — qualitative characteristic — reports must be
prepared in sufficient time to form the basis of effective
decisions.

Transaction — economic or financial event in the life of a
business

Two-fold effect of transactions — every transaction has
two effects on the affairs of a business.

Variance — difference between the actual amounts and
the budgeted amounts on the accounting reports.

Working capital ratio - measures the relationship
between the current assets and current liabilities of the
business,

GLOSSARY

Account — a record of transactions of a particular type
Accounting equation — A= +P, or P=A—L
Accrued expense ~ an expense that is incurred before it
is paid

Accrued revenue — revenue that is earned before it is
received

Accumulated depreciation — the total of the
depreciation that has been written off from a non current
asset

Allocated cost ~ the total depreciation which has been
written off against revenue (accumulated depreciation)
Bad debts — amounts that cannot be collected from
debtors

Balance-day adjustments — adjustments prepared at the
end of the accounting period so that the principle of
accrual accounting is adhered to (so that the results for
the accounting period reflect the activity which actually
took place)

Balancing ~ calculation and recording of the balance of
an account

Carrying value ~ the written down value of a non current
asset

Cash payments journal — a record book used for all
payments of cash by the business

Cash receipts journal ~ a record book used for all
receipts of cash by the business

Closing entries — entries in the general journal and
ledgers required to prepare the ledger for the following
accounting period

Control account — an account in the general ledger that
summarises the accounts in a subsidiary ledger

Credit — item which is recorded on the left hand side of
an account

Debit ~ item which is recorded on the right hand side of
an account

Depreciation — allocation of the cost of a non current
asset against revenue

Discount allowed (expense) ~ a reduction in the amount
payable by debtors if they pay their accounts within a
specified period. An inducement to settle debts promptly
Discount received (revenue) — a reduction in the
amount payable to a creditor if the account is paid within
a specified period.

Double entry — system used for the recording of
transaction in a ledger. Two entries are made for each
transaction

FIFO — First In First Out — system of recording and stock
management that uses the oldest stock on hand when
sales are made

Financing activities — a classification of the statement of
cash flows which covers loan borrowing and repayments,
cash contributions of capital, and cash drawings of capital
Folio numbers — cross-references inserted into the
ledger to show the source of the information, and into the
journals to show the destination of the information
Footing — Calculation of the balance of an account
General journal — a record book used for transactions
that are infrequent

Goods and Services Tax ~ a tax levied by the Australian
Government on the supply of goods and services
(currently 10%). A value added tax.

Identified cost ~ a system of stock recording and stock
management where each item is tagged and identified
with the actual cost

Investing activities — a classification of the statement of

© Blake Education ISBN 978 1 92253 853 6

cash flows which covers cash paid for new non current
assets and proceeds from sale of non current assets
Ledger — book of accounts ~ a book used to record all of
the transactions that have been summarised into
separate accounts.

Non-recurring entries — entries in a general journal —
transactions which occur infrequently therefore do not
have a special journal

Opening journal entry — an entry in the general journal
to establish the existing balances for the double entry
system

Operating activities — a classification of the statement of
cash flows which covers all cash transactions for trading
activities - cash sales and collections from debtors, cash
expenses and payments to creditors

Prepaid expense — an expense that is paid before it is
incurred

Prepaid revenue — revenue that is received before it is
earned

Purchases journal ~ a book used to record all
purchases of trading stock on credit

Purchases returns (returns out) — goods returned to
suppliers

Reducing balance depreciation — a method of
calculating depreciation based on the written down value
(carrying value) of the asset

Residual value (scrap value) ~ the difference between
the cost of a non current asset and the accumulated
depreciation which has been written off so far.

Sales journal ~ a book used to record all sales of trading
stock on credit

Sales returns (returns in) — goods returned by
customers

Statement of cash flows — statement that includes all
cash flowing into and out of an entity during an
accounting period, classified into operating, investing and
financing activities

Statement of financial performance ~ (Statement of
profit and loss) statement including all revenues and
expenses for an accounting period and showing the profit
of loss for the period

Statement of financial position (Balance sheet) ~
statement including all assets and liabilities and giving
proprietorship as a residual amount, prepared on a
particular date

Stock card — a record of all movements of stock into and
out of the business

Stock gain — the total value of stock in the warehouse is
greater than the value of stock in the records

Stock loss — the total value of stock on the records is
greater than the value of the stock in the warehouse
Stock take — counting and valuing of stock owned by the
business

Stock write down — a downward adjustment in the value
of the stock

Straight line depreciation - a method of calculating
depreciation based on the cost of the asset

Subsidiary ledger — books kept to record the detail of
the balances in the control account in the general ledger
(used for debtors, creditors and stock)

Transactions — an economic or financial event in the life
of the business

Trial balance ~ a listing of all of the balances in the
ledger to check that the total of the debits equals the total
of the credits

4 SUBSIDIARY LEDGERS/CONTROL ACCOUNTS

Terms you should know

Creditors control account — an account in the general ledger that summarises the transactions that have
been recorded in detail in the creditor's subsidiary ledger

Creditors subsidiary ledger — a ledger that contains all the details of transactions with the individual creditor.
Debtors control account — an account in the general ledger that summarises the transactions that have been
recorded in detail in the debtor's subsidiary ledger

period. An inducement to settle debts promptly.

Discount received — a reduction in the amount payable to a creditor if the account is paid within a specified
period.

Purchases returns — goods returned to suppliers

Sales returns — goods returned by customers

11 SPECIAL JOURNALS with GST

Terms you should know.

Cash payments journal — a record book used for all payments of cash by the business

Cash receipts journal — a record book used for all receipts of cash by the business

Creditors schedule — a list of balances from the creditors subsidiary ledger. The total of the individual creditor
balances must agree with the balance of the control account.

Debtors schedule — a list of balances from the creditors subsidiary ledger. The total of the individual debtor
balances must agree with the balance of the control account.

Goods and Services Tax (GST) — a tax levied by the Australian Government on the supply of goods and
services (currently 10%). A value added tax.

Purchases journal — a book used to record all purchases of trading stock on credit

Sales journal — a book used to record all sales of trading stock on credit

Subsidiary ledger — books recording the detail of the balances in the control account in the general ledger
(used for debtors, creditors and stock)

Terms you should know

business (the business makes no profit or loss)
Contribution margin – the amount that each item sold contributes towards the expenses of the business.
Selling price less variable costs (cost of purchasing the items).
Desired profit – the amount that the business hopes to earn after all costs have been met
Fixed cost – a cost that will not vary with the number of items sold eg wages, electricity
Variable cost – the cost of buying in item for sale. Total variable costs will differ with the level of activity of the
business.

Contribution margin = selling price – variable cost

Terms you should know
Continuous recording – ongoing recording of the stock or inventory (manually using stock cards or using technology)
First-In-First-Out (FIFO) – a stock management system where the oldest stock is the first to be sold
Identified cost – a stock management system where all items of stock carry a tag showing the cost price of the item
Inventory – stock held by the business for resale
Lead-time – the time it takes for stock that has been ordered to arrive at the business
Perpetual recording – each purchase or sale (and return) is recorded at cost price at the time of transaction

Stock card – a manual record of all movements of stock into or out of the business

Terms you should know
Accumulated depreciation – total of depreciation that has been written off so far
Allocated cost – the amount of the original cost which is written off over the useful life of the asset
(depreciation)
Carrying value – the cost of an asset less the accumulated depreciation (written-down value)
Depreciable value –
Depreciation – the allocation of the cost of a non-current asset over its effective working life
Reducing-balance method – a method of calculating the depreciation of an asset based on the carrying value
(written-down value) at the end of the previous period
Straight-line method – a method of calculating the depreciation of a non current asset by allocating the cost
evenly over the useful working life
Written-down value – the cost less accumulated depreciation of a non current asset (carrying value)

Terms you should know
Accrual basis of reporting – profit or loss is calculated taking into account all revenues earned and expenses incurred
for the accounting period, whether or not they have been received or paid
Accrued expenses – expenses that are incurred before they are paid (these are liabilities)
Gross profit – the difference between the sales revenue and the cost of goods sold. It is available to cover the cost of
other expenses and for net profit.
Net profit – sales revenue less all expenses incurred in earning that revenue. Net profit increases owner’s equity.
Prepaid expenses – expenses that are paid before they are incurred (these are assets)
Statement of financial performance (Profit and loss statement) – a statement reporting on all of the revenues and
expenses incurred by an entity in an accounting period. It is a summary statement.
Statement of financial position (Balance sheet) – a statement reporting all of the assets and liabilities of an entity and
showing the owner’s equity (proprietorship). It is a position statement.

Glossary
Contribution margin – the amount that each item
sold contributes towards the expenses of the
business. Selling price less variable costs (cost of
purchasing the items).
Cost of goods sold – the total costs related to the
goods that have been sold. Sales revenue less cost
of goods sold equals gross profit.
Credit transactions – sale or purchase of goods or
services where no cash changes hands at the point
of sale.
Creditor – supplier of the goods or services that
have been purchased on credit.
Creditors schedule – list of amounts owing to
creditors for the credit purchase of goods or
services
Current assets – items of value owned or
controlled by the business that are cash or will be
turned into cash within a period of 12 months
Current liabilities – amounts owed by the
business that must be paid within a period of 12
months
Debtor – customer who has purchased goods or
services on credit
Debtors schedule – list of amounts owed by the
debtors (accounts receivable)
Deposits not credited – amounts which have been
received by the business but have not yet been
banked (are not recorded on the bank statement)
Depreciation – the allocation of the cost of a non
current asset over its effective working life
Desired profit – the amount that the business
hopes to earn after all costs have been met.
Direct deposits – amounts that are deposited
directly into the bank account.
Discount allowed – an inducement to a debtor to
get them to pay their account quickly.
Discount received – offered by the creditor as an
inducement to pay the account quickly
Drawings – amounts of cash or other assets
withdrawn from the business by the owner
Fixed cost – a cost that will not vary with the
number of items sold eg wages, electricity
Entity assumption – the affairs of the business
and the affairs of the owner must be kept separate
Expenses – costs incurred in the process of
earning revenue
FIFO – First In, First Out – a stock management
system where the oldest stock is the first to be sold
Goods and services tax (GST) – a value added
tax which must be added to the selling price to get
the price which must be paid by the customer.
Currently GST is 10%

Accounting equation – expresses the relationship
between the amounts owned by the business and
the amounts owed by the business. Usually
expressed as A = L + P or A = L + OE (owner’s
equity).
Accounting period (reporting period) – the period
for which accounting reports are prepared. This
cannot be longer than 12 months.
Accounts payable – amounts owing by credit
customers
Accounts receivable – amounts owing to credit
suppliers
Accrual basis of reporting – profit or loss is
calculated taking into account all revenues earned
and expenses incurred for the accounting period,
whether or not they have been received or paid
Accrued expenses – expenses that are incurred
before they are paid (these are liabilities)
Accrued revenues – revenues that are earned but
not yet received (these are assets)
Accumulated depreciation – total of depreciation
that has been written off so far
Allocated cost – the amount of the original cost
that is written off over the useful life of the asset
(depreciation)
Assets – item of financial value owned or
controlled by the business, it has future benefits for
the business.
Bad debts – an amount that will not be received
from a credit customer
Balance sheet – Statement of financial position – a
statement reporting all of the assets and liabilities
of an entity and showing the owner’s equity
(proprietorship)
Bank reconciliation – the process of checking the
bank balance in the records of the business against
the bank balance as shown by the bank
Breakeven – the point at which all of the costs of
the business are covered by the revenue of the
business (the business makes no profit or loss).
Carrying value – the cost of an asset less the
accumulated depreciation (written-down value)
Cash flow statement – a statement showing all
cash inflows less all cash outflows
Cash payments – cash outflows of the business
Cash payments journal – book used to record the
cash outflows of the business
Cash receipts – cash inflows of the business
Cash receipts journal – book used to record the
cash inflows of the business
Continuous recording – ongoing recording of the
stock or inventory (manually using stock cards or
using technology)
© Blake Education   ISBN  978 1 92561 072 7

Gross profit – the difference between the sales
revenue and the cost of goods sold. It is available
to cover the cost of other expenses and for net
profit.
Identified cost – a stock management system
where all items of stock carry a tag showing the
cost price of the item.
Imprest system – system for recording of petty
cash
Income – revenue derived from the trading
operations of a business
Inventory – stock held by the business for resale
Lead time – the time it takes for stock which has
been ordered to arrive at the business
Liabilities – amounts owed by a business
Mark up on cost – a calculation of the selling price
of an item, based on the cost price plus a
percentage to cover other costs.
Net profit – sales revenue less all expenses
incurred in earning that revenue. Net profit
increases owner’s equity.
Non cash expenses – expenses such as
depreciation or bad debts for which no cash is paid
out.
Non current assets – items of value owned or
controlled by the business which will be of benefit
to the business for a period longer than 12 months
Non current liabilities – amounts owed by the
business which will not need to be paid within the
next 12 months
Payments – outflows of cash from the business
Payments by authority – payments made by the
bank on the authority from the account holder
Perpetual recording – continuous recording of
stock or inventory – each purchase or sale (and
returns) is recorded at cost price at the time of
transaction.
Petty cash – small amounts of cash used to pay
for expenses that cannot be paid by cheque.
Petty cash advance (float) – the amount that is
kept in the petty cash fund.
Prepaid expenses – expenses that are paid before
they are incurred (these are assets)
Prepaid revenues – revenues that are received
before they are earned (these are liabilities)
Profit and loss statement – Statement of financial
performance – a statement reporting all of the
revenues and expenses of an entity in an
accounting period
Purchases journal – book used to record the
credit purchase of goods or services
Purchases returns – stock returned to the supplier
Receipts – inflows of cash to the business
Reducing-balance method – a method of
calculating the depreciation of an asset based on
the carrying value (written-down value) at the end
of the previous period.
Reimbursement – the cheque drawn to bring the
petty cash balance back up to the imprest amount
Reporting period – accounting period – the period
for which accounting reports are prepared. This
cannot be longer than 12 months.
Returns in – stock returned to the business by a
customer
Returns out – stock returned to the supplier
Revenue – income earned from the operations of
the business
Sales journal – book used to record the credit sale
of goods or services
Sales returns – stock returned to the business by
customers
Single entry recording – a recording system
which has one entry for a transaction, usually in a
cash book. Subsidiary records may also be
maintained.
Statement of cash flows – a statement reporting
on all of the inflows and outflows of cash for an
entity, classified as operating, investing and
financing operations
Statement of financial performance – Profit and
loss statement – a statement reporting on all of the
revenues and expenses incurred by an entity in an
accounting period. It is a summary statement.
Statement of financial position – Balance sheet –
a statement reporting all of the assets and liabilities
of an entity and showing the owner’s equity
(proprietorship) It is a position statement.
Statement of receipts and payments – a
statement reporting all of the inflows and outflows
of cash in an accounting period. It is a summary
statement.
Stock card – a manual record of all movements of
stock into or out of the business
Stock loss – recorded stock is greater than the
stock on hand as per the stock take.
Stock take – counting of stock on hand in a
business for the purpose of calculating and
accurate gross profit
Straight-line method – a method of calculating the
depreciation of a non current asset by allocating the
cost evenly over the useful working life
Trading statement – a statement showing details
of the sale of goods and the cost of goods sold,
used to calculate the gross profit.
Unpresented cheques – cheques that have been
written out but have not yet been presented to the
bank for payment.
Variable cost – the cost of buying in item for sale.
Total variable costs will vary with the level of
activity of the business
Working capital – difference between current
assets and current liabilities. Amounts available for
payment of short term liabilities.

1945: World War II ends. The Allies (United 
States, Great Britain, Soviet Union,

Japan)

cull rabbits

Many Indigenous Australian people are 
affected by radiation and forced from 
their land.
1962: Indigenous Australian people are 
given the right to vote in federal elections. 
1965: Freedom Ride. Bus ride through NSW 
to investigate how Indigenous Australian 
people were treated
1966: Currency changes from the Imperial 
system of pounds and shillings like Britain 
to dollars and cents like America.

would be paid the same amount as men 
for doing the same work.
1970: Vietnam War protests held in most 
capital cities

largely destroyed.
1976: First boat people arrive, escaping 
Vietnam after the war. More Asian 
migration follows. 
1983: Ash Wednesday bushfires kill 72 
people and destroy 2000 homes.
1984: Advance Australia Fair becomes the 
national anthem
1992: Mabo decision. Lands right case for 
Indigenous Australian people; terra nullius 
(empty land) defence is  overturned
2001: The World Trade Center in New York 
was attacked by terrorists; almost 3000 
died.
2006: Commonwealth Games held in 
Melbourne
2009: Black Saturday. Massive bushfires 
throughout Victoria kill 173 people.
2014: Sydney hostage crisis. A man took 
18 people hostage at the Lindt Cafe in 
Sydney. The man and two hostages were 
killed.

Resource sheet – Music
Bill Haley vs The Beatles
In 1957, Australia faced a huge rock’n’roll experience when American band Bill Haley & His 
Comets came to Australia. Many parents were concerned that bands like this would turn 
their children into rebels and criminals. In 1964, this fear was increased by the extreme 
Beatlemania of the fans when British band The Beatles came to Australia for the first time.
Source 1 
But Bill Haley who wants to see rock‘n’roll catch on in Australia, doesn’t want to see riots. 
‘I never HAVE seen riots,’ pronounced big smooth-faced Bill Haley who sports a C (for 
Comet) shaped lock of hair down the centre of his forehead. ‘Let me tell you about some 
so-called riots… Inside the Ballpark where we were playing were 11,000 kids, Outside 
because they didn’t have the money to go in were two teenagers. When the police asked 
the two kids to move off, these two kids smashed a soft drink bottle against a wall … 
All seven of the Comets are married – six out of the seven are fathers.’
Helen Frizell, ‘Please no riots says American Rock’n Roll King’, Australian Women’s Weekly, 
23 January 1957
Source 2 
In June 1964, The Beatles toured Australia. Huge numbers of fans turned up to their 
performances, flight arrivals and even their hotel rooms. This obsessional fan behaviour 
was labelled ‘Beatlemania’. Over 30,000 people waited to catch a glimpse of The Beatles 
when they performed at the Town Hall in Adelaide. At the time, the band said that this was 
the largest welcome they had ever received. When The Beatles performed, audiences were 
often so loud with their screaming, stamping and singing that many people could not 
actually hear the band playing.
Rachel Towns, Achieve History: Pop Culture 1945–present, Blake Education, 2018
Source 3 
Parents who always moan about their teenagers listening to Beatle records don’t seem to 
remember that when they were young they listened to songs with titles like ‘Marsey Doats 
and Dosey Doats’.
Songs like this weren’t even based on a good story, so please ‘Marsey Doaters’ give 
The Beatles a fair go. Join in and you’ll soon be enjoying singing their bright clear songs 
also – Beat Teen Mount Gambier S.A
‘Mad Oldies’ Letters’, Australian Women’s Weekly, 10 June 1964
Reproduced with permission 
from Bauer Media Pty Limited / 
The Australian Women’s Weekly

In 1971, Australian songwriter Helen Reddy

In 1983, Redgum released the song ‘A walk in the

John Schumann, the lead singer, used his own 
experiences as a Vietnam veteran to write the song.

In 1991, Indigenous Australian band Yothu Yindi 
released their song ‘Treaty’. This song focused

Australian peoples. It is about the hope for a 
treaty between the Australian government and 
Indigenous Australian peoples to begin addressing 
the racial inequality in Australia.
3  A treaty is a legal agreement 
between two groups. Why 
do Yothu Yindi and other

Australian film industry
Resource sheet – Cinema and censorship
1900s–1920s: Innovation
In the 1900s, anyone could enter 
the film industry if they could buy 
the equipment. Most films were 
‘one-reelers’ which meant they 
were only about 12 minutes long. 
The Australian film The Story of the 
Kelly Gang (1906) was the first full-
length feature film in the world.
1940s–1960s: Imitation
Australian–British or Australian–American 
films such as The Sundowners (1960) were 
made in Australia. Uniquely Australian films 
were less common and often centred on 
stereotypical Australiana like the kangaroo in 
Skippy and the Intruders (1969). One exception 
was Jedda (1955) which was the first film to 
star two Indigenous Australian actors. Another 
was They’re a Weird Mob (1966). This was a 
comedy that explored the problems that Italian 
migrants encountered in Australian society.
1970s: Golden years
In the 1970s, the Australian 
government realised that the film 
industry needed their support. 
Many films made in the 1970s 
were ocker adventures like The 
Adventures of Barry McKenzie (1972) 
which relied on stereotypes and 
rude humour. Other films were 
more literary and artistic, like 
Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975). The 
critical success of these films paved 
the way for the funding of more 
popular films like Mad Max (1979).
1980s–1990s: Australia goes international
In the 1980s, Australian films like Mad Max 2 
(1981) and Crocodile Dundee (1986) became 
very popular overseas. Australia was idealised 
as an exciting, exotic location. This image of 
glamour extended into the 1990s with the 
ballroom dancing in Strictly Ballroom (1992), 
ABBA’s music in Muriel’s Wedding (1994) and the 
drag queens of The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen 
of the Desert (1994). These films showcased a 
very different version of Australia. 
Australia in the 21st century
Many films made in the Australia in the 2000s and 2010s focused on Australian 
criminality: serial killers, families of criminals and hitmen. These films included Chopper 
(2000), Wolf Creek (2005) and Animal Kingdom (2010). However, there have also been 
heart-warming stories about unlikely heroes and underdogs such as The Sapphires (2012), 
The Dressmaker (2015) and Lion (2017).

Censorship and classification
Censorship is when someone controls what you can read, write, listen to or watch. When you 
were a child, your parents may have stopped you from watching shows that were intended 
for adults. This is a kind of censorship.
+  1  Cross out the incorrect words in bold so that the information about censorship 
make sense.
Activity sheet – Cinema and censorship
The Australian government has censored / supported materials over the years, usually 
due to violence, sexuality or political views. Censored materials cannot / must be 
published or distributed. Some people approve of this as they believe it protects people 
from boring / dangerous material. Other people disapprove of censorship because it 
means they must / cannot make their own decisions about what they read, watch or play.
In 1929, Lady Chatterley’s Lover by D. H. Lawrence was censored / published because of its 
sexual content. 
In the 1969 case Crowe vs Graham, four men were fined for publishing / hiding parts of 
censored books. 
Because of the Graham case, in 1972 the government / cinemas began using a 
classification system instead of censoring / giving materials. This system tells you which 
materials are suitable for different audiences: G (General, suitable for everyone), PG 
(Parental Guidance recommended), M (Mature, recommended for people aged 15 and 
over), MA 15+ (restricted to people aged 15 and over), R18+ (Restricted to people aged 18 
and over) and RC (Refused Classification – banned).
In the 2000s, some gamers made compliments / complaints because games were being 
banned / sold due to extreme cuteness / violence, sexuality and other problematic 
content. Some games that were originally rated as RC and celebrated / banned were 
permitted under a R18+ rating in 2011.

b  When do you think books, movies or games should be censored?

Melbourne Olympics
In 1956, the Summer Olympics were held in Melbourne, Australia. This was an important time 
for Australia – for the first time, elite athletes travelled from all over the world to compete 
in Melbourne and Ballarat. Television was introduced to Australia that same year so people 
could watch the races instead of just listening to them on the radio.
+  1  Highlight the keywords in the source below. Keywords are the important words 
that tell you what a sentence is about. The first paragraph has been done for you. 
Women and Olympics
After almost four years of bickerings, recriminations and gloomy forebodings of one kind 
or another, the Olympic year has finally dawned – and peacefully at that.
It is now pretty certain, come what may, nothing can take the Olympic Games from 
Melbourne. For the first time in history, Australia in staging games with almost 3000 years 
of tradition behind them, is about to enjoy a spot of the glory that was Greece.
We suspect, though, that this glory as Melbourne will see it would cause a sharp shift of 
amazement to the classic eyebrow of any ancient Greek …
The Grecian village of Olympia was off-limits to women. On pain of death, no female 
dared show her nose inside Olympia even as a spectator, let alone as a competitor. 
It is true that one determined type, undoubtedly the spiritual ancestress of all feminists, did 
get herself not only into the village, but also into a chariot race which she had the tactlessness 
to win.
This finished the Games as far as Greek women were concerned. But obviously not as far 
as Australian women are concerned.
They are taking an almost 50–50 part in these Games as competitors, as organisers, as 
hostesses, as officials. 
That they will fully justify the responsibilities given them we have no doubts at all. And in 
doing so they’ll demonstrate one glory that Greece never knew – the equal rights of women.
‘Women and the Olympics,’ The Australian Women’s Weekly, 18 January 1956
2  Write a paragraph about how the involvement of women in the Olympics changed 
from Ancient Greece to Melbourne in 1956 to now. You could research the most recent 
Olympics to help you write in more detail.

Fiction
Before films, the internet and video games, books were the main way of telling stories in our 
society. They are still important, not only for the stories they tell, but also for what they say 
about the time that they were written.  
Puberty Blues by Gabrielle Carey and Kathy Lette was published in 1979. It is an 
autobiographical story about their experiences as 13-year-old girls who wanted to  
fit in with the surfing culture of Sydney.
+  1  What is happening in the quote?
 
 
 
 
2 a  How is language used by the writer? Highlight these words in the quote to help you:  
•  chirping       •  chicks      •  little black bikinis           •  flocked.
 
 
 
 
 
b What is the effect on the reader of using language in this way?
 
 
3 a How are females represented in this quote?
 
 
 
b What does this tell you about the way the writers saw themselves?
 
 
4 What does this quote tell you about the time the book was written?
 
 
 
 
Definitions
grounded: punished by 
being made to stay home
chirping: a happy sound 
made by a bird
flocked: moved in a large 
group (often refers to 
birds)
T he beach was the centre of our world. Rain, snow, hail, a 
two-hour wait at the bus stop, or being grounded, nothing 
could keep us from the surf. Us little surfie chicks, chirping 
our way on the train. Hundreds of us in little white shirts, 
short-sleeved jumpers, thongs, straight-legged Levis covering 
little black bikinis. We flocked to the beach. Cheep. Cheep.
From Puberty Blues by Gabrielle Carey and Kathy Lette, Text Publishing Company and 
Random House Australia, 2012, p. 1.

Changes in the home, changes in our world
In the past women were expected to stay at home to look after  
their family and to cook and clean. Over time, appliances such  
as vacuum cleaners, washing machines, ovens and microwaves  
became more advanced and quicker and easier to use.
Many women found it easier to get an education and a job  
outside the home when they did not have to spend so much  
time cooking and cleaning. They also had more time to  
consume popular culture in the form of films, books and music.
+  Use a search engine to explore how housekeeping technology  
has changed since 1945. Use search phrases such as ‘washing machine history’.
1 What has changed about washing clothes?
 
 
 
 
2 What has changed about how we cook food?
 
 
 
 
3 What has changed about the way floors are cleaned?
 
 
 
 
4 Are there any elements of these devices that have stayed the same? Why?
 
 
 
 
5 How do you think popular culture influenced the purchase and use of these machines?
 
 
 
 
 
 
6  In your workbook, make an annotated drawing of a home appliance from the year 2060. 
What features of your invention might give families more leisure time?

Entertainment
With the development of technology, 
entertainment activities moved from reading, 
writing and playing to listening to radio and 
finally to watching television.
Television was introduced in Australia at the 
same time as the Melbourne Olympics in 1956. 
This meant that people could now see the events 
as well as listen to them. 
At first, there were three channels: ABC (originally 
ABN), Nine (originally TCN-9) and Seven (HSV7). 
Channel Ten was introduced in 1964. In 1980, the 
SBS channel was created to broadcast content 
targeted at multicultural audiences. 
To support Australian culture and identity, the 
Postmaster General decided in 1960 that 40% of 
programs on Australian television channels had 
to be made in Australia.
+  1 What did people do for entertainment before television? 
 
 
2 What has changed about television channels over the decades? 
 
 
 
 
3 Who decided there should be Australian content on television? Why?
 
 
 
 
4 Which event in the television timeline do you think is the most important? Explain why.

Bodgies, widgies and surfies
There have always been groups of people that wear similar clothes, listen to the same music 
and act in the same way. In the 1950s there were the bodgies (boys) and widgies (girls).  
In the 1960s and 1970s, there was the surfie culture.
Bodgies and widgies – 1950s
•   Adopted American culture
•   Rock’n’ roll music like Bill Haley & His 
Comets
•   Hung out at milk bars and went to dances
•   Boys: hair in a ducktail style, wore leather 
jackets and denim jeans
•   Girls: short hair, wore stight black skirts 
with loose shirts
•   Some were seen as rebellious youth 
misbehaving
Surfies – 1960s and 1970s 
•   American / Australian culture
•   Surf music like The Beach Boys
•   Hung out at the beach and went surfing
•   Boys: dyed their hair blonde, wore board 
shorts with thongs and sometimes a polo 
shirt
•   Girls: long blonde hair, bikinis with jeans 
and white shirts
•   Often drove panel vans
•   Seen as shiftless and lazy, focusing on fun 
rather than acting like adults
+  1  Imagine you are a bodgie or widgie. Write a diary entry about a typical weekend. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 Write a diary entry about life as a surfie.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3  What culture groups are there today? What do they look like? What do they listen to, 
play and watch? Make a list in your workbook.

Different views: Vietnam
Parents and children often think differently and have very 
different views on a particular issue. Part of this is due to  
growing up in different generations with different experiences.
+  Read what Doreen and Michael have to say about conscription and the Vietnam War. 
Conscription: When the 
government needs soldiers 
and makes a law to say 
that if you can fight, you 
have to join the military.
I can’t go and fight. I just can’t. T hey sent me my draft card the 
other day. My numbers had come up in the lottery for National Service 
and suddenly I have to go to another country and kill people who have 
never done anything to me. I’m not afraid. I know I will go to jail 
for this and I am not afraid of that. But – I am afraid of not being 
a good man. Of going to another country and forcing those people to be 
something other than what they want to be. You don’t see the politicians 
going over to fight, but they tell us that we should go, and be proud. 
Well I am not proud. I cannot be proud of a country that does this.
Reading the newspaper, I can scarcely believe the world we are living 
in. When my father was a young man he fought for our country. He 
He was only 19 and fought in the jungles of Borneo. Now with the 
Vietnam War and the fight against communism, we have all these kids 
trying to tell us that it is a ‘dirty war’. T hey’re just cowards. You didn’t 
hear my dad complaining about being sent away to war. Now these boys 
are going around, burning their draft cards, saying they don’t have to 
go. Makes you ashamed to be an Australian.
Michael
Doreen

5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Human rights
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Background
Racism has long been a key element of our world. 
European countries like England and Spain invaded 
numerous countries in Africa, Asia and America in the 
15th and 16th centuries. They used their perception 
of racial superiority to justify their mistreatment 
of native people. In the 18th and 19th centuries in 
Australia, Indigenous peoples were forced off their 
land because they did not use the land as Europeans 
did. In other countries such as India, white people were 
automatically given the best jobs and opportunities, 
Anglo-Indians, (half-British, half-Indian) were given 
middle-ranking positions, while the lowest positions 
were reserved for Indians. This racism was also 
entrenched in America where legislation allowed 
for ‘separate but equal’ toilets, water taps and other 
facilities for white and black people. 
As part of the Paris Peace Conference (1919–20), the 
question of a Racial Equality clause was introduced 
by Japan. The Japanese saw themselves as a superior 
race that had quickly modernised in the 20th century 
to keep up with Europe and America. Japan had also 
supported the Allies (England, France and America) 
in World War I because Germany tried to take land 
claimed by Japan. However, Australian Prime Minister 
Billy Hughes wanted to maintain the racial exclusivity 
of the White Australia Policy (Immigration Restriction Act 
1901) and blocked a racial equality clause that might 
challenge the ‘whiteness’ of Australia. 
After World War II, the situation on the world stage 
was different. Racial issues that were easily dismissed 
after World War I were now centre stage. No-one could 
deny that the German’s genocidal treatment of Jews, 
Gypsies, Slavs and other groups deemed ‘subhuman’ 
(Untermenschen) by the Nazis had a racial factor. The 
introduction of the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights on 10 December 1948 was a move towards 
improved human rights.
Starter activity
Have the students work in small groups, and provide 
each group with poster paper. Ask each group to 
identify the rights that they think everyone in a society 
should have. The students should also explain the 
reasons for their choices.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘League of Nations’, looks at Japan’s  
attempt to introduce a racial equality clause into the 
key legal documents of the Treaty of Versailles at the 
1919 Paris Peace Conference. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Racial Equality Proposal’, follows 
on from the previous Activity sheet by exploring the 
different attitudes of Japan and Australia towards this 
proposal. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Eleanor Roosevelt and Herbert 
Evatt’, students are introduced to two key people who 
contributed to the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights’, identifies key features of this document. On the 
Activity sheet, ‘My rights’, students use the Resource 
sheet to help them develop their own Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights.
Extension ideas
Imagine that you are creating your own society.
• What laws would you make?
• What would you do with people who broke the 
rules?
• What rights do you think everyone should have?
• In what situations would you treat people 
differently? Why?
Objectives
• Consider the role of the League of Nations 
and the United Nations in the development of 
human rights
• Learn about changes in perspectives about 
race over the 20th century
• Develop an understanding of key legal 
documents

17
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – 1900–1965
Prior knowledge
Students may benefit from a knowledge of interactions 
between British colonists and Indigenous Australian 
peoples prior to 1901.
Background
As part of the Federation of Australia, legislation that 
reinforced the secondary position of Indigenous 
Australian peoples was introduced. These changes 
were embedded within the Constitution, which is 
the central document that shaped the formation of 
Australia as a nation. Relevant changes include the 
decision not to count Indigenous Australians in the 
census (the document that records the population of 
Australia) and the Commonwealth Franchise Act of 1902 
which prohibited Indigenous Australians from voting 
in Federal elections. This meant they had no legal 
opportunities for resistance and representation. At the 
same time, women were given the right to vote. This 
clearly demonstrates the attitudes of the time. 
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, there was 
a theory that Indigenous Australian peoples were 
a ‘doomed race’. Authorities of the time may have 
believed it was unnecessary to include in the census a 
race that would soon be extinct.  
These changes served to remove Indigenous Australian 
peoples from the political and legal sphere. They were 
treated as children; unable to make political, economic 
or social decisions for themselves or for the nation. 
In the late 1800s, Aboriginal Boards were established in 
most states. These boards attempted to act as ‘parents’ 
to the Indigenous Australian peoples. Someone under 
their authority often had to apply to the board to 
obtain wages, ask for permission to marry or to visit 
friends and relatives in different reserves. 
The restrictions on the lives of the Indigenous 
Australian peoples varied from state to state. But one 
thing remained the same – their lives were limited 
simply because of their race.
Starter activity
Consider what it is like to have someone else make all 
the important decisions for you: where you must live, 
where you can go, how much money you have and 
what kind of work you can do. Is it fair? What would it 
be like if this control continued for your entire life?
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Aboriginal Boards’, provides 
information about the restrictions on the lives of 
Indigenous Australian peoples in Australia. Students 
will refer to this information in as they complete the  
Activity sheet, ‘Restricted lives’. Here, students interpret 
the information from the table and make general 
statements based on the data. Then they write a 
creative response about life for Indigenous Australian 
people in 1960.  
On the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous Australian Anzacs’, 
students explore the treatment of Indigenous 
Australian soldiers and nurses in different wars. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Soldiers and nurses’, follows on 
from the previous Activity sheet. Here, students use 
primary source images to identify key features about 
the wars and how Indigenous Australian people were 
represented and treated during these wars. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Source: Half-blood to octaroon’, 
uses a specific photograph to explore views of 
interracial relationships. Students will use the 
information on this Resource sheet to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘CHIPS analysis’. Here, they analyse the 
source photograph and consider the context of the 
time in which it was published, 1947.
Extension ideas
Ask students to research life on a reserve in the 1940s 
to 1960s. Website suggestions:
•    Lake Tyers, Victoria 
indigenousrights.net.au/land_rights/lake_
tyers,_1962-70/early_history_of_lake_tyers
•    Moore River Settlement, Western Australia 
www.noongarculture.org.au/moora
•    Bamaga, Queensland 
https://www.qld.gov.au/atsi/cultural-awareness-
heritage-arts/community-histories-bamaga
Have students write a report about their findings. 
Objectives
• Consider the treatment of Indigenous Australian 
peoples prior to the 1967 Referendum
• Consider how the institutionalisation of racism 
that occurred with Federation impacted on the 
lives of Indigenous Australian peoples 
Web addresses were functional at the time of 
publication but teachers should check them for 
inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

24
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Working for change
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of the European 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples may be 
useful.
Background
Many Indigenous Australian people were unhappy with 
their situation after European settlement. They had 
been moved away from their land – their food places, 
sacred spots and familiar locations. The European 
colonists fenced off the best land for their farms. 
Indigenous Australian peoples were moved to less 
desirable land and often to reserves and missions. 
Federation brought with it legislation that reinforced 
the secondary position of Indigenous Australians. 
They were excluded from the census and banned from 
voting.
Many Indigenous Australians began fighting for their 
rights. They formed groups, identified significant days, 
compiled petitions, established a ‘tent embassy’ and 
organised strikes. 
One significant figure in this early resistance period is 
William Cooper. He began a protest group and made 
many deputations. He also organised the first Day of 
Mourning on 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary of 
colonisation.
Cooper was unusual because he was one of the few 
Australians to protest at the German Consulate in 
Melbourne about the treatment of Jewish people 
before World War II. At this time, many nations would 
not even accept Jewish refugees, let alone condemn 
Germany’s actions.  
Starter activity
Paul Kelly’s song ‘From little things, big things grow’ 
tells the story of Vincent Lingiari and the strikes at Wave 
Hill Station. Play the song for the class. Then lead a 
group discussion about the story told in the song and 
why it is important.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource Sheet, ‘Protection, assimilation, 
integration and self-determination’, identifies different 
ways in which Indigenous Australian peoples were 
viewed and treated in Australian society. 
Students use the information from the Resource 
sheet to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Where do 
we fit?’. Here, students create a cartoon to explain 
each term: protection, assimilation, integration and 
self-determination. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Profile: William Cooper’, looks at one 
of the most significant pre-1945 Indigenous Australian 
civil rights figures. As an extension activity, students 
could research how William Cooper’s actions led to 
today’s NAIDOC week.
The Activity sheet, ‘Civil rights actions’, highlights some 
of the actions of Indigenous Australian civil rights 
groups. Students will use complete a timeline showing 
key events. 
Students will use the previous Activity sheet to help 
them complete the Activity sheet, ‘Petition for change’. 
Here, students identify a significant modern issue and 
write a petition to fight for change. You could have 
students work in pairs or small groups to complete this 
activity.
Extension ideas
Have students choose a key Indigenous Australian 
figure, group or protest to research. 
Ideas:
• Fred Maynard
• William Ferguson
• Australian Aborigine’s League
• Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association
• Tent Embassy
• Day of Mourning
The students should identify and briefly describe their 
topic, then explain why the topic is significant to the 
Indigenous Australian Civil Rights movement.
Objectives
• Consider the policies of assimilation and 
integration
• Identify some of the early Indigenous 
Australian protest groups and explore the ways 
they fought for change

ACHIEVE!   History: Rights and freedoms
36
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Fighting for change
Prior knowledge
Students may benefit from an understanding of the 
American Civil Rights movement in the 1950s and 
1960s (See previous unit: Civil Rights movement, USA).
Background
After World War II, people became more concerned 
about the treatment of different races and religious 
groups. This new awareness was matched in a number 
of countries by increasing civil rights actions.
In the United States, there had long been groups like 
the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement 
of Colored People). But it was only in the 1950s and 
1960s that their actions began having a wider impact. 
Their attempts to fight for political rights through 
court cases, petitions, boycotts, Freedom Rides and 
sit-ins had an enormous impact. There is still racial 
discrimination and inequality there today, although the 
situation has greatly improved.
In Australia in the 1950s and 1960s, there was also 
an increasing concern about racial discrimination. A 
number of groups began protesting about the unequal 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples: the use 
and abuse of reserves, restrictions on who they could 
marry and what they could drink, minimal access to 
education and limited political representation. 
 Many Indigenous Australian peoples looked to the 
large and powerful civil rights groups in America for 
ideas on how to protest. They also used Freedom 
Rides, protest marches and court cases to fight 
for the same rights as other Australians. In 1949 
Indigenous Australians were officially made citizens 
but the changes to their rights were limited. In 1962, 
Indigenous Australians were finally allowed to vote 
in Federal elections. There was a Referendum in 
1967 where everyone voted on whether Indigenous 
Australian people should be included in the census 
and whether special laws just for Indigenous Australian 
people should be abolished. Ninety percent of 
Australians voted for these changes. 
Starter activity
You could watch ‘Eyes On The Prize (Part 3):  
Ain’t Scared of Your Jails, 1960–1961’ (55 mins),  
www.youtube.com/watch?v=neDpuJVc4Ko with the 
students. This documentary shows what the US Civil 
rights experience was like, with an emphasis on sit-ins 
and Freedom Rides. Make sure you review the movie 
first as there is violence and students may find some 
scenes disturbing. 
Alternatively, choose stills from this documentary or 
other relevant images of sit-ins or Freedom Rides. Lead 
a class discussion about how effective these ways of 
protesting were.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Looking to America for ideas’, 
discusses Australia’s links to the United States and asks 
students to match protest terms and definitions.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Freedom Rides’, students are 
given information about the Freedom Rides in Australia 
and map the journey taken by one group. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Charles Perkins and Ann Curthoys’, 
provides information about two Freedom Riders and 
primary sources about their experiences. 
Note: Perkins’ source uses the term ‘nigger’. Make 
sure that students understand that this is a historical 
term and very much outdated in usage. It was highly 
offensive at the time and still is today. 
Students use the Activity sheet, ‘Free riders – source 
analysis’, to guide them through the process of 
analysing the sources on the previous Resource sheet. 
Make sure the students understand that bias means 
that a persons shows a prejudice towards (likes or 
dislikes) a group of people.
The Activity sheet, ‘Aims, tactics and outcomes’, looks 
at other protest actions of Indigenous Australian civil 
rights groups.
Extension ideas
Go onto trove.nla.gov.au and research references 
to the Australian Freedom Rides in the 1960s in the 
newspapers. Use terms like ‘Freedom Rides’ or ‘Freedom 
Riders’ to help you find information. 
• What is happening in the article?
• How is the situation represented?
• Include a quote and explain what it means.
Objectives
• Identify the actions of the Indigenous 
Australian Indigenous Civil Rights movement 
during their protests 
• Consider how the Indigenous Australian Civil 
Rights movement was influenced by the US 
African-American Civil Rights movement

42
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Restrictions and rights
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge about the position of 
Indigenous Australian peoples before Federation and 
the social changes in the 1960s may be useful.
Background
In the 1960s, a number of social issues began to 
rise in prominence. Racism, sexism, militarism and 
homophobia became issues that were challenged 
by different groups in society. The horrors of World 
War II had awakened the world to the potential 
consequences of viewing groups of people as ‘lesser’. 
This led to the creation of the United Nations Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. This document 
identified the rights that all humans deserved, 
regardless of their background or beliefs. 
The idea that all people should have certain rights 
was revolutionary. Even in the 1940s and 1950s, black 
and white people were still segregated in America, 
coloured people (African and Indian) were living under 
Apartheid in South Africa and Indigenous Australian 
peoples were kept in reserves and controlled with 
special laws in Australia. 
During this time, women were also dealing with sexist 
attitudes that limited their opportunities for education 
and employment. Homosexuals were treated with 
prejudice and faced dangerous consequences if their 
sexuality was revealed. This was also the time of the 
Cold War, which was a battle of communism (led by the 
Soviet Union) and capitalism (led by the United States).
In response to these challenges, society began moving 
away from its rigid traditional social behaviour and 
more people began questioning the status quo. One 
aspect of this was the hippy movement of the 1960s 
which focused on a lifestyle outside of the norm. But 
there were many others. Peace groups protested about 
wars in Korea and Vietnam, the women’s liberation 
movements fought against sexism, the civil rights 
movements challenged the racist ideas that skin colour 
shaped ability, personality or intelligence, and, later on 
in the 1970s, people fought for gay rights. All of these 
groups and movements challenged the traditional 
structure of society. In many ways, the fight for the 
rights of one group contributed to the fights for the 
rights of other groups.
Starter activity
Watch a documentary about the 1967 Referendum. 
Suggestions:
•   1967 Aboriginal Timeline – Introductory cultural 
competency module 
www.youtube.com/watch?v=gXVVDG_NFaQ (3 mins)
•   We Made History in the 1967 Referendum  
www.youtube.com/watch?v=qasH5oJiSaU (4 mins)
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Changing rights’, provides a useful 
overview of the restrictions placed on Indigenous 
Australian peoples in the key areas of the census, 
voting and special laws. Students research quotes to 
support the facts provided in the voting and special 
laws sections. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Essay plan’, students are guided 
through the process of creating an essay plan using the 
information from the Activity sheet, ‘Changing rights’. 
Discuss the TEEEM structure with the class, especially 
if students have not used it before. As an extension 
activity, students can use their plan to write an essay.
TEEEM Paragraph Plan
Always start with a topic sentence and always end with 
a mini-conclusion. Put the evidence, explanation and 
essay keywords in the middle.
• T – Topic sentence: introduce your specific topic
• E – Evidence: to support your ideas
• E – Explain: your ideas in your own words
•  E – Essay keywords: use keywords from the essay 
question and the topic sentence to show you are 
answering the question
•  Mini-conclusion: sum up what you said in that 
paragraph.
Extension ideas
Have students write their own essay question, based on 
their knowledge of the rights of Indigenous Australian 
people. Make sure they use task words such as: discuss, 
justify, identify, explain, compare or contrast. Students 
could then prepare an essay plan for the question.
Objectives
• Consider how Indigenous Australian peoples 
were restricted around Federation
• Identify how Indigenous Australian peoples 
gradually regained rights in the 1960s
• Plan and write an essay on a historical issue

49
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – The Stolen Generations
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of the European 
treatment of Indigenous Australian peoples may be 
useful.
Background
Indigenous Australian peoples often experienced 
prejudice and discrimination from the first days of 
the arrival of Europeans in Australia. This prejudice 
included removal from their land, beatings, being sent 
to reserves, rape and massacres. Many Europeans felt 
justified in their treatment of Indigenous Australian 
peoples because they believed that the colour of their 
skin showed that Indigenous Australians were lesser 
people in terms of ability, intelligence and character. 
Under the protectionist policies of the colony 
governments, most Indigenous Australians were 
removed to reserves. On the reserves, they were taught 
English, European farming methods and enough 
skills to serve white people as labourers and domestic 
servants. The view of the colony governments was that 
Indigenous Australians were like children who needed 
to be protected by white people.
In the 1930s, many governments moved towards a 
policy of assimilation. They still believed that people 
with darker skin were lesser beings and needed to be 
protected like children, but they began to treat children 
with both Indigenous Australian and European parents 
as different to those of ‘pure’ Indigenous Australian 
ancestry. These children were often taken from their 
homes and immersed in white Australian culture. 
The children affected by this policy later became 
known as ‘the Stolen Generations’. This was the 
dominant policy from the 1930s to the 1970s, although 
children may have been taken before and after this 
period. 
Starter activity
Have the class watch Philip Noyce’s film, Rabbit-proof 
fence (2002). It is based on the true story of three 
Indigenous Australian girls who are taken from their 
families, escape, and then make the long journey back 
home. The film is adapted from the book written by 
Doris Pilkington Garimara, the daughter of one of the 
girls in the story. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Children of our blood’, explores the 
situation for people with both Indigenous Australian 
and European parents. Make sure the students 
understand that bias means that a person shows a 
prejudice towards (likes or dislikes) a group of people.
The Resource sheet, ‘Stolen children’, provides four 
primary sources that relate to the Stolen Generations in 
Australia. 
Students use the Resource sheet with the Activity 
sheet, ‘Plan a story’, to help them plan a story about the 
Stolen Generations.
The Activity sheet, ‘Bringing Them Home report’, 
provides information about the inquiry into the Stolen 
Generations that was completed in 1997. Students will 
answer questions about the inquiry and some of the 
recommendations made in the report. 
Extension ideas
Use the library or internet to find further primary 
sources about the Stolen Generations. Students could 
also look for primary sources that relate to reuniting 
the families who were separated in this time.
Students could present their findings as a poster or a 
multimedia presentation.
Objectives
• Consider how Indigenous Australian peoples 
were treated in Australia
• Explore the treatment of Indigenous Australian 
children
• Plan and write a historical story
The terms ‘half-caste’ and ‘full-blooded’ were once commonly used. Today, they are highly offensive, especially to 
Indigenous Australian peoples. These terms are linked to the historical belief that people of different racial groups 
should not marry nor have children – a racist idea that is considered completely unacceptable in today’s society.

54
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2018
Teacher’s notes – Native title
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge about the treatment 
of Indigenous Australian peoples in Australia may be 
useful.
Background
In the 1960s Indigenous Australian people were 
granted the right to citizenship and inclusion in 
Australian society. In 1962, Indigenous Australians were 
given the right to vote in Federal elections which finally 
allowed for the possibility of Indigenous Australian 
representation. This was followed in 1967 by the 
overwhelmingly successful Referendum in which 90% 
of Australians voted ‘yes’. This Referendum changed 
the Constitution so that Indigenous Australians would 
be included in the census (the collection of data 
about the population of Australia). It also removed the 
rights of states to enforce special laws for Indigenous 
Australians. These laws had meant that Indigenous 
people could have different rights, depending on the 
specific laws of the state they lived in.
This did not mean that racial equality had been 
established. Although institutional racism had been 
challenged, it was just the beginning of a much larger 
battle against racism which continues to this day.
The British designated Australia as terra nullius (empty 
land) to justify their colonisation and settlement of 
a land that belonged to other people. This decision 
meant that successive governments had no problem 
with removing Indigenous Australian peoples 
from their land. Indeed, they saw themselves as 
compassionate for placing Indigenous Australians 
in reserves and ‘caring’ for them. The reserves were 
generally on poor quality land that was not suitable for 
European use. 
This view of Australia as empty land was challenged 
through legal cases like that of Eddie Mabo. His case 
ran from 1982 to 1992 and became known as the Mabo 
case. The High Court recognised that native title existed 
and that Indigenous Australian peoples had rights to 
their land. 
Similarly, the 1990s brought a rising concern about the 
need for reconciliation and a national apology. Steps in 
this process include the introduction of National Sorry 
Day in 1998. This is now a day of commemoration held 
on 26 May each year. 
Starter activity
Lead a class discussion about the historical problems 
that Indigenous Australian people faced (e.g. rape, 
murder, attacks, prejudice, sent to reserves, rights taken 
away).
Discuss how this past treatment of Indigenous 
Australian peoples affects all Australians today. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Eddie Mabo’, introduces important 
elements of his life and his fight for Indigenous 
Australian rights. 
Students use this Resource sheet to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘The Mabo case’. Here, students learn 
more about the political and social background to 
the Mabo case and write a paragraph about the 
implications of Eddie Mabo’s victory.  
On the Activity sheet, ‘Native Title Act 1993’, students 
compare and contrast two key native title cases: the 
Mabo case and the Wik decision. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Reconciliation’, leads students 
through the process of making a timeline of key events 
relating to reconciliation. 
Tthe Activity sheet, ‘National Sorry Day’, focuses on 
Kevin Rudd’s apology speech in 2008. Students then 
write their own apology speech to the Indigenous 
Australian people.
Extension ideas
Have students work in pairs or small groups. Ask them 
to use http://trove.nla.gov.au to find newspaper articles 
about Eddie Mabo or National Sorry Day.
Students should:
•  choose one newspaper article
•  identify the views reflected in the article 
•   discuss the bias (prejudice for or against) of the writer, 
using supporting evidence from the article
•  suggest reasons for the writer’s bias.
Objectives
• Consider key events in modern history that 
have contributed to the fight for the rights of 
Indigenous Australian peoples 
• Learn about the significance of National Sorry 
Day and the Mabo case
